title: Choose the new settings direction
question: Which way should scrnsvr make choosing a shader feel? Each direction keeps the live preview and all existing settings.

options.label: The Slide Table
options.lineage: A projectionist's illuminated slide sorting table
options.thesis: The shader collection is a set of luminous slides you can immediately project and adjust.
options.viewport: A visible strip of shader frames sits beside a large live projection; a compact inspector stays at the far edge. The selected frame joins the projection with one clear selection line.
options.risk: Its analog reference must remain subtle enough that the live shader stays the most vivid element.

raised.raise: Controls get the deck's precise, labeled physical rhythm without chrome decoration.
Each shader frame has its own unmistakable visual identity, even when small.
Rotation uses a legible ordered sequence beneath selection, rather than buried checkboxes.
A disciplined alignment rail ties the selected frame, preview, and inspector together.
Generous clear ground around shader imagery makes color differences easy to judge.

options.label: The Visual Mixer
options.lineage: A VJ's live visual mixing desk
options.thesis: Choosing a shader feels like cueing a visual on a performance desk.
options.viewport: A large live output sits over a bank of category-organized visual tiles, with a persistent right-hand channel strip for shader controls and clock settings.
options.risk: It is the familiar direction for visual software and could feel too technical for casual selection.

options.label: The Light Stage
options.thesis: Shader choices become lighting cues, with the live canvas treated as the stage.
options.viewport: The live shader fills a stage-like central frame; an always-visible cue list lets people compare named shaders, while the adjustment bank reads as a lighting console.
options.case: Its atmospheric language fits scrnsvr, but a cue list makes visual comparison less immediate than a slide table.
options.risk: A stage metaphor may imply show sequencing beyond the actual rotation feature.

options.label: Cassette Deck
options.lineage: A cassette futurist tape deck fascia
options.thesis: Each shader occupies a labeled instrument channel on a hardware fascia.
options.viewport: A control deck surrounds a large output display.
options.case: Precise controls fit tuning, but tape hardware identifies less clearly with visual shader discovery.
options.risk: Physical chrome could compete with the actual shader imagery.

options.label: Pixel Metropolis
options.thesis: An isometric shader city invites zooming into visual worlds.
options.viewport: Shader scenes live as blocks in a zoomable city.
options.case: Its authored character is memorable, but it hides accurate shader previews behind an unrelated city interaction.
options.risk: The city overwhelms the actual WebGL output.

options.label: Rhythm Machine
options.thesis: A step row makes shader rotation tangible.
options.viewport: Shader choices form a row of cue keys under a live output.
options.case: The sequence maps well to rotation, but most users first want to select and preview one shader.
options.risk: The step interface might suggest unsupported beat editing.

options.label: Emission Rail
options.thesis: Shader selections register as spectral lines along one calibration rail.
options.viewport: A selected shader blooms from a calibrated rail into a live plate.
options.case: Its calibration rigor resonates with shaders, but line marks are weak substitutes for visual thumbnails.
options.risk: The collection becomes harder to browse by eye.
options.kept: Align selection, preview, and controls to one rail.

options.label: Cloud Quarry
options.thesis: Visual atmospheres are cut and assembled as material blocks.
options.viewport: Weather-like slabs become shader choices around a live output.
options.case: The visual idea is striking, but sculpting clouds does not match choosing existing shaders.
options.risk: It implies a shader composition feature the product does not offer.

canonCard.label: The Familiar Gallery
canonCard.thesis: A polished dark settings app with the expected preview, grid, and inspector.
canonCard.viewport: Large live preview on the left, dense tuning controls on the right, shader cards organized below.
canonCard.risk: The collection remains below the first screen and looks similar to today's UI.
